kurals.tamil:
காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும்
நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamak kanichchi utaikkum niraiyennum
naanuththaazh veezhththa kadhavu.
kurals.meaning: My reserve was a door shut fast with the bolt of modesty, but the axe of love smashes that door down.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a girl who keeps her feelings locked behind a strong door, with shyness as the bolt. But her love for someone is like a big axe, and one swing breaks the whole door open. Feelings that strong cannot stay locked away.
kurals.university: Chapter 126, niṟai aḻital (‘the breaking of reserve’), opens with the heroine (talaivi), parted from her husband, admitting that the self-command she prized has given way. The image is architectural: niṟai (reserve, the firmness that keeps inner feeling from showing) is the door (katavu), nāṇ (modesty, shame) is the bolt (tāḻ) that holds it, and kāmam (love-longing) is the kaṇicci, a heavy axe or pick, which breaks it; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss kaṇicci as an axe (கோடாலி/கோடரி). In the reading associated with Parimelazhagar, niṟai is the faculty that guards what should be kept within and nāṇ is its fastening, so the couplet states the chapter’s claim that love overpowers both together. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. Textual note: ytamizh.com’s English ‘Couplet Explanation’ for 1251 (‘My precious life is saved by the raise of rumour…’) does not fit this couplet and appears to be misplaced from another kural; its Pope couplet (‘The axe of lust can break the door of chastity…’) is the relevant rendering.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The senses are so strong and impetuous, O Arjuna, that they forcibly carry away the mind even of a man of discrimination who is endeavoring to control them.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that even a wise person who is trying to stay in control can have his mind seized by the force of the senses.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine had the same careful control, and love carries it off by force like an axe through a bolted door.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.60 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; strong match on self-control overpowered, though the Gita speaks of the senses in general rather than of love for a spouse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him. I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock.”
christianity.explanation: The bride, already settled for the night, is so moved by her beloved’s hand at the door that she rises to unbolt it.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts use a bolted door to picture a woman’s reserve, and in both love gets through it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); the door-and-lock image matches closely, though the bride opens the door willingly rather than having it broken.

islam.quote_or_event: “And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She closed the doors and said, ‘Come, you.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells how the wife of al-Aziz, overcome by longing for Joseph, set aside her position and modesty.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows love breaking down a woman’s reserve; here the same passion overrides a noblewoman’s dignity, though the Qur’an condemns her intent.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); shares the theme of passion overriding modesty, but the context is an illicit pursuit that Joseph refuses, so the moral frame differs sharply.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…for love is strong as death, jealousy is cruel as the grave; the flashes thereof are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it…”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs declares love a force as unstoppable as death that nothing can put out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s axe expresses the same conviction: no bolt of modesty can hold love back.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a close match on love’s irresistible power, though the Song does not speak of breaking reserve.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, so passion penetrates an undeveloped mind.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares an untrained mind to a badly roofed house that passion gets into as easily as rain.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts picture the self as a house that passion breaks into; the Buddha’s answer is to train the mind, while the Kural’s heroine simply admits the house has been breached.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the house image and passion breaking through are a close match, though the Buddhist aim is to prevent the breach, not to describe a beloved’s power.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi’s strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion.”
jainism.explanation: In a cave on Mount Raivataka, the monk Rathanemi’s resolve gives way on seeing Rajimati, while she keeps hers.
jainism.tie_back: Rathanemi is the Kural’s broken door in a monk’s robe: his will is broken by passion, exactly the collapse of niṟai the heroine describes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a direct picture of willpower broken by passion, though Jain scripture presents it as a monk’s lapse to be corrected, not a lover’s confession.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho says that Eros the limb-loosener shakes her once again, a bittersweet creature against which there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek lyric, Eros is a force that seizes the lover from outside and undoes her body and composure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sappho and the Kural’s heroine both describe love as an attacker that breaks through a self-possession they cannot defend.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous two-line fragment; a strong match on love as an overpowering force, though Sappho uses the image of loosened limbs rather than a broken door.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will, and that reason is, and ought only to be, the servant of the passions.
philosophy.explanation: Hume denies that calm reasoning can stand guard against a strong passion on its own.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same point in a lover’s terms: the reasoned restraint of niṟai cannot hold against love.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; good fit on passion overruling restraint, though Hume is making a general claim about motivation, not about love.

kurals.tamil:
காமம் எனவொன்றோ கண்ணின்றென் நெஞ்சத்தை
யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamam enavondroa kannindren nenjaththai
yaamaththum aalum thozhil.
kurals.meaning: This thing called love has no pity: even at midnight, when everyone else rests, it keeps ordering my heart about.
kurals.elementary: Think of a strict boss who makes you work even in the middle of the night while everyone else is asleep. The heroine says love is like that boss: it never lets her heart rest, not even at midnight.
kurals.university: The heroine personifies kāmam as a harsh ruler: kaṇ iṉṟu means ‘without kaṇṇōṭṭam’ (without kindly regard, pitiless), as Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதது), and yāmattum āḷum toḻil is ‘the work of ruling even at yāmam’, the dead of night. Solomon Pappaiah draws out the image of a master who makes a servant toil at midnight while all others sleep, which sharpens the chapter’s theme: niṟai cannot survive a power that never rests. The phrase eṉa oṉṟō (‘this one thing called…’) carries a note of exasperated contempt in the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads kaṇ iṉṟu as ‘standing in the eye’ (கண்ணில் நின்று), a minority interpretation. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On a bright autumn night the gopis of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute and, leaving whatever they were doing, run to him through the dark, unable to stay at home.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows love for Krishna taking command of the gopis precisely at night, overriding every household duty.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the gopis find that love rules their hearts at the hour when all others rest.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; strong on love’s night-time command, though the Bhagavata reads it as devotion to God and the gopis go joyfully, not as servants of a pitiless master.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh.”
christianity.explanation: The bride is asleep, yet her heart stays awake, listening for her beloved at night.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also finds that her heart cannot rest at night; love keeps it at work.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close match on a heart kept awake by love at night, though the Song is tender where the Kural calls love pitiless.

islam.quote_or_event: Nizami tells how Qays, separated from Layla, roams the desert by night and day, so mastered by his love that he loses his name and is called Majnun, the madman.
islam.explanation: In the Persian romance, love becomes a ruler that leaves the lover no rest and no command over himself.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says love rules her heart even at midnight; Majnun’s love rules him so completely that it costs him his reason.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the widely known story, not checked against a translation this session; good fit on love as an all-hours master, though Majnun’s state is far more extreme.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: In the night the woman of the Song cannot sleep; her longing sends her searching for the one she loves.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise finds love at work in her heart in the middle of the night.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); close match on night-time longing, though the Song’s voice is searching rather than complaining.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lord, as I was leaving home, a Sakyan girl — the envy of the countryside — glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, ‘Hurry back, master.’ Recollecting that, I don’t enjoy leading the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother, tells the Buddha that the memory of his betrothed has such a hold on him that he cannot keep up his monastic life.
buddhism.tie_back: Nanda’s heart, like the heroine’s, is governed by love even when everything around him calls for calm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; strong on love’s hold over the mind, though the sutta says nothing of night, and the Buddha goes on to free Nanda from it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Haṭha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati warns the monk Rathanemi that a mind ruled by desire has no anchor and is pushed wherever passion blows it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes exactly such a mind: love rules it at every hour, and she has lost her hold.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a real image of a mind driven by desire, but it is a rebuke to a fickle monk rather than a faithful wife’s complaint, and it has no night-time element.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After first seeing Jason, Medea lies awake through the night: sleep will not come to her, her heart throbs like sunlight flickering on water in a pail, and she turns her choices over and over until dawn.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius gives one of ancient literature’s fullest portraits of a young woman whose love keeps her awake and torments her at night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Medea’s sleepless heart is the Kural’s heart ruled by love even at midnight.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.744-801 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; very close on night-time torment by love, though Medea’s conflict also involves betraying her father.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the lover, parted from the beautiful one, is in such distress that he can neither sleep by night nor stay quietly in one place by day, but runs wherever he hopes to see the beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes love as a restlessness that takes away the lover’s sleep and composure.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels the same: love will not let her heart rest even at midnight.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Jowett tradition; a close match on sleeplessness caused by love.

kurals.tamil:
மறைப்பேன்மன் காமத்தை யானோ குறிப்பின்றித்
தும்மல்போல் தோன்றி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Maraippaenman kaamaththai yaanoa kurippindrith
thummalpoal thoandri vidum.
kurals.meaning: I try to hide my love, but it gives no warning; like a sneeze, it simply bursts out.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever tried to stop a sneeze in a quiet room? You hold your nose, but out it comes anyway. The heroine says her love is like that: she tries to keep it secret, but it pops out all by itself.
kurals.university: The homely simile of the sneeze (tummal) is one of the most memorable images in the Kāmattuppāl: the heroine would conceal (maṟaippēṉ) her kāmam, but it appears kuṟippiṉṟi, ‘without regard to my intention’ or ‘without warning’. The particle maṉ in maṟaippēṉmaṉ marks an intention that fails (‘I would indeed hide it, but…’), a construction repeated in 1254 (eṉpēṉmaṉ). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses kuṟippiṉṟi as ‘not staying as I intend’ (என் குறிப்பின்படி நிற்காமல்), while Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘without my even knowing’, stressing involuntariness. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘like a sneeze / It shows itself, and gives no warning sign’) keeps the image. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Act 3 of Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala, wasting with love for King Dushyanta, tries to keep her feelings to herself, but her friends Anasuya and Priyamvada read the signs on her body and draw the confession from her.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa shows a young woman’s love becoming visible to those around her despite her silence.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s sneeze, Shakuntala’s love shows itself before she chooses to reveal it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; a close fit on love betraying itself, though Shakuntala is not yet married.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, which bewrayeth itself.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says some things simply cannot be hidden: trying is like hiding the wind, or perfume on your hand that gives itself away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s sneeze is the same kind of image: something that reveals itself however you try to hide it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close on the impossibility of concealment, though the proverb is about a contentious woman, not about love.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm devotes chapters to the signs of love and to the keeping of the lover’s secret, observing that lovers try to hide their passion but are betrayed by their glances, their confusion and their changing colour.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian treatise on love treats concealment as a duty the lover attempts and often fails.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine attempts the same concealment, and her love likewise breaks through without warning.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapters on the signs of love and on concealing the secret (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the treatise’s general argument, not checked against Arberry’s text this session; strong thematic fit on love betraying itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And if I say: ‘I will not make mention of Him, nor speak any more in His name’, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I weary myself to hold it in, but cannot.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah resolves to stay silent, but what is in his heart forces its way out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine resolves to hide her love and likewise cannot hold it in.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); the experience of failing to hold something in matches closely, but the prophet’s fire is God’s word, not love for a person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, King Sivi glimpses the beautiful Ummadanti and is so struck that he cannot hide his condition: he becomes lovesick and absent-minded, and his longing becomes plain to those around him.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka shows a king’s concealed passion making itself known despite his position and self-command.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the king finds that love shows itself without his consent.
buddhism.source: Ummadanti Jataka (Jataka 527) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the general outline of the Jataka, not checked against Cowell’s text this session; the theme of love that cannot be hidden fits, but the story’s moral turns on the king mastering an improper desire.

jainism.quote_or_event: When the monk Rathanemi sees Rajimati sheltering in a cave from the rain, his peace of mind is disturbed and he at once speaks his desire aloud to her, unable to keep it to himself.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana shows a disciplined monk whose sudden passion breaks out in words the moment it arises.
jainism.tie_back: Rathanemi’s passion, like the heroine’s love, bursts out before restraint can contain it.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.33-38 (paraphrase of tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of verses read on sacred-texts.com; the sudden uncontainable outburst fits, but the Jain text treats it as a moral lapse, unlike the Kural’s sympathetic heroine.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, Phaedra explains that she first tried to bear her love in silence and hide it, then to master it by self-control, and only when both failed resolved to die rather than be shamed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides dramatizes a woman’s doomed effort to conceal a love that keeps showing itself in her wasting body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaedra’s first strategy is the Kural heroine’s ‘I would hide it’, and both find that love will not stay hidden.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Hippolytus, Phaedra’s speech to the women of Troezen (c. lines 373-430; paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known speech; strong on failed concealment, though Phaedra’s love is forbidden and tragic, unlike the heroine’s love for her husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that there is no disguise that can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
philosophy.explanation: The French moralist states as a general maxim that real love cannot be kept hidden.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sneeze turned into a maxim: love reveals itself whatever the lover intends.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in idea; given as paraphrase because the wording and maxim number were not checked against a live text this session.

kurals.tamil:
நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன் யானோஎன் காமம்
மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Niraiyutaiyaen enpaenman yaanoa-en kaamam
maraiyirandhu mandru patum.
kurals.meaning: I used to tell myself I had firm self-control, but my love has broken out of hiding and now shows itself in the public square.
kurals.elementary: Imagine being sure you could keep a big secret, and then finding the whole town talking about it. The heroine thought she was strong enough to keep her love quiet, but now everyone can see it.
kurals.university: The heroine contrasts what she used to say (niṟaiyuṭaiyēṉ eṉpēṉmaṉ, ‘I would say I have reserve’, the maṉ again marking a claim now undone) with what happens: her kāmam, passing beyond concealment (maṟai iṟantu), appears in the maṉṟu, the village common or assembly place. The word maṉṟu makes the exposure social: her longing is now matter for public talk, recalling the alar (gossip) of chapter 115. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss maṉṟam as the public assembly; Solomon Pappaiah renders the result as ‘known to the townspeople’ (ஊரவர் அறிய). Pope’s English on ytamizh.com (‘In womanly reserve I deemed myself beyond assail; / But love will come abroad, and casts away the veil’) brings out the gendered sense of niṟai in the commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar. The couplet is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In her letter to Krishna, Princess Rukmini writes that, having heard of his qualities, her heart has set aside shame and entered into him, and she asks him to carry her off before her unwanted wedding.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata presents a high-born maiden openly declaring a love that propriety would have kept hidden.
hinduism.tie_back: Rukmini’s love, like the heroine’s, passes beyond concealment and declares itself.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.52.37-43 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known letter, not re-checked verse by verse this session; good fit on love overriding modesty, though Rukmini’s disclosure is a deliberate choice rather than an involuntary exposure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him… And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard.”
christianity.explanation: Joseph has long hidden who he is from his brothers, but his feeling finally bursts out so loudly that all Egypt hears it.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a restraint the person relied on gives way, and the feeling becomes public.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a vivid match on restraint breaking in public, though the love is a brother’s, not a lover’s.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-’Azeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an records how a noblewoman’s hidden passion for Joseph became the talk of the city’s women.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds exactly this: her love has left its hiding place and become public talk.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); very close on hidden love becoming public gossip, though the Qur’an condemns her passion as wrongful.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, what will ye tell him? that I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song no longer hides her state; she tells the women of the city outright that she is sick with love.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also finds her love has gone beyond concealment and become known to others.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); good fit on love made public, though in the Song it is an open declaration rather than an unwilling exposure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Venerable Nanda, they say, has been hired. Venerable Nanda, they say, has been bought.”
buddhism.explanation: When it became known that Nanda was keeping the holy life only for the sake of the promised nymphs, his fellow monks went around saying this, and he was humiliated and ashamed.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the heroine, Nanda finds that the longing he kept inside has become the common talk of his whole community.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the exposure-and-shame pattern fits, but Nanda’s motive is a promised reward, not love for a spouse, and the shame leads him to liberation.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Sutrakritanga warns that when relations and friends see a monk becoming intimate with a woman, they grow angry and openly tell him that, being a man, he should protect and support her.
jainism.explanation: The Jain text shows a monk’s concealed attachment exposed to public judgement.
jainism.tie_back: Like the heroine, the monk who thought himself restrained finds his attachment has become known to all.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 1.4.1.14 (paraphrase of tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verse read on sacred-texts.com; it shares only the motif of hidden attachment becoming public, and its monastic warning is far from the Kural’s sympathy for a wife.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the minstrel Demodocus sings how Hephaestus caught Ares and Aphrodite together in an invisible net and then called the gods to come and see, so that their secret love was exposed before the company of Olympus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s comic tale shows a hidden love dragged into public view.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences the same thing in gentler form: her love has left its hiding place and stands in the public square.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.266-366 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; it matches the image of love exposed in public, but the affair is adulterous and the tone comic, so the fit is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the person who lacks self-control knows what is right, but under passion holds that knowledge only as a drunk or sleeping man holds it, like someone reciting verses of Empedocles without understanding them.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle explains how a person who believes himself self-controlled can still be overrun by passion.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘I used to say I had reserve’ is a lover’s version of Aristotle’s akrasia: her restraint existed, but passion overrode it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VII.3, 1147a (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous argument; it fits the failure of self-command but not the public exposure the Kural stresses.

kurals.tamil:
செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை காமநோய்
உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Setraarpin sellaap perundhakaimai kaamanoai
utraar aRivadhondru andru.
kurals.meaning: The dignity that refuses to run after someone who has turned away is something those sick with love simply do not know.
kurals.elementary: When a friend walks away from you, pride might say, ‘Fine, I won’t chase after them.’ But the heroine says that when you love someone very much, that kind of pride disappears, and you want to follow them anyway.
kurals.university: Ceṟṟār, literally ‘those who hate’ or ‘enemies’, is here the husband who has gone away, seen through the heroine’s hurt as one who has spurned her; peruntakaimai is the noble self-respect (Mu. Varadarasanar: மானத்தோடு நிற்கும் பெருந்தகைமை) of not following such a person. Kāmanōy uṟṟār, ‘those who have caught the sickness of love’, do not know that dignity, so the couplet extends the chapter’s theme from concealment to pride. Commentators divide on the logic: Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take it as a direct statement that the lovesick lack such dignity, Solomon Pappaiah turns it around (only those who have not known love can manage it), and Kalaignar stresses that the lovesick cannot treat the departed lover as an enemy. In the reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the heroine is explaining to her confidante why she cannot simply hold her ground. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Mirabai sings that for the sake of her Giridhar (Krishna) she has thrown off family honour and the shame the world expects of a noblewoman, and goes after him whatever people say.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti poet makes a virtue of the loss of decorum that the Kural’s heroine confesses.
hinduism.tie_back: Both women find that love leaves no room for the dignified reserve society expects.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, padas on abandoning lok-lāj (family honour) (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Alston)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a recurring theme in the Mira tradition rather than one verified pada; strong on abandoning dignity for love, though Mira’s beloved is divine and never spurns her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, a father who has every reason to stand on his dignity runs to the son who left him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, the father cannot keep the dignified stance of not going after one who went away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); the loss of dignity out of love fits, but it is a father’s love and the son is returning, not spurning.

islam.quote_or_event: “She said, ‘That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he firmly refused…’”
islam.explanation: Before the women of the city, the wife of al-Aziz openly admits that she pursued Joseph even though he refused her.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the lovesick lack the dignity of not following one who turns away; here a noblewoman confesses to exactly that loss.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); fits the pursuit of one who refuses, but the Qur’an presents it as wrongdoing, so the moral frame is opposite.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I will rise now, and go about the city, In the streets and in the broad ways, I will seek him whom my soul loveth.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song gives up all reserve and goes out through the city streets at night to look for her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise cannot keep the dignity of staying put; love sends her after the one who has gone.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); close on giving up reserve to pursue the beloved, though the beloved has not spurned her.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises against binding oneself to anyone, because separation from the beloved is itself suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows the pain this verse foresees: the one who loves cannot stand apart from the beloved, even with dignity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it diagnoses the same bondage, but offers detachment as a cure, which the Kural’s heroine does not seek.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Fie upon you, famous knight, who want to quaff the vomited drink for the sake of this life; it would be better for you to die.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, herself forsaken by Arishtanemi, rebukes his brother Rathanemi for pursuing her, keeping her dignity and her vows.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati shows the dignity the Kural says the lovesick cannot have; her strength comes from having turned her grief toward renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; an illustration by contrast, since Rajimati keeps the dignity the Kural’s heroine has lost.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo falls in love with Narcissus and secretly follows his footsteps through the woods; when she shows herself he recoils and spurns her, yet she keeps loving him, wasting away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the classic story of a lover who cannot stop following the one who rejects her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo is the Kural’s lovesick heroine in mythic form: she does not know the dignity of not following one who turns away.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a close match on following one who spurns, though Narcissus was never Echo’s husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates says the lover forgets mother, brothers and friends, cares nothing if his property is wasted, and despises all the rules and proprieties of life on which he once prided himself, ready to sleep wherever he is allowed, as near as he can to his beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes love as a madness that strips the lover of the dignity and decorum he once valued.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same admission: the lovesick do not know the dignity of holding back.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 252a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Jowett tradition; a near one-to-one match on love overriding a person’s former pride and propriety.

kurals.tamil:
செற்றவர் பின்சேறல் வேண்டி அளித்தரோ
எற்றென்னை உற்ற துயர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Setravar pinsaeral vaendi aliththaroa
etrennai utra thuyar.
kurals.meaning: What a strange grief has seized me, that it makes me long to follow the very one who has turned away from me!
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when a friend goes away, we feel so sad that we want to run after them, even if they did not say a kind goodbye. The heroine wonders at this sadness: it is so strong that it makes her want to follow him anyway.
kurals.university: The heroine marvels at her own grief: eṟṟu (‘of what kind?’) and the exclamatory aḷittarō, which can be heard ironically as ‘how gracious!’, frame a sorrow (tuyar) that makes her wish to go after (piṉ cēṟal) ceṟṟavar, the one who has scorned or left her. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘My grief how full of grace, I pray you see! / It seeks to follow him that hateth me’) captures this irony. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan treat tuyar as the kāmanōy (love-sickness) itself, and Solomon Pappaiah calls it exceedingly cruel because it drives her to follow. The couplet continues 1255: having denied that she has the dignity not to follow, the heroine now wonders at the grief that compels her. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna suddenly disappears from the rasa dance, the gopis, stricken with grief, search the forest for him, asking the trees and creepers whether they have seen him pass.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows women whose grief at their beloved’s withdrawal sends them looking for him everywhere.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the gopis are driven by grief to follow the one who has left them.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.30 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous chapter; strong on grief that seeks the departed beloved, though in the Bhagavata Krishna withdraws to humble the gopis’ pride, not out of scorn.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: When the bride finally opens the door, her beloved has gone, and she goes searching and calling for him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also longs to follow the one who has turned away, and wonders at the grief that drives her.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match on following one who withdrew, though the bride’s beloved has not scorned her.

islam.quote_or_event: “Barira’s husband was a slave called Mughith, as if I am seeing him now, going behind Barira and weeping with his tears flowing down his beard. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to ’Abbas, ‘O ’Abbas! are you not astonished at the love of Mughith for Barira and the hatred of Barira for Mughith?’”
islam.explanation: After Barira, newly freed, chose to leave her marriage, her husband Mughith followed her through the streets of Medina in tears.
islam.tie_back: Mughith is the Kural’s lover exactly: grief makes him follow the one who has turned away, and the Prophet himself remarks on the wonder of it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a near one-to-one match on grieving pursuit of a spouse who has turned away.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The watchmen that go about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my mantle from me.”
judaism.explanation: Searching through the city for the beloved who has gone, the woman of the Song is beaten and stripped of her mantle, yet keeps searching.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also marvels at a grief that makes her follow the one who left, whatever it costs her.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); fits the painful pursuit of a departed beloved, though the verse stresses its cost rather than the grief behind it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From lust springs grief, from lust springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to desire and attachment.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences what this verse names: her grief comes from a longing that drives her after the one who has gone.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the analysis fits, but the Buddha prescribes freedom from craving where the Kural’s heroine only marvels at her grief.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi on their wedding day, Rajimati follows him into renunciation and later sets out for Mount Raivataka, where he had gone.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s grief, like the heroine’s, makes her follow the one who left her, though she follows him on the path of renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong on grief that leads her to follow the one who left, though Jain tradition turns her following into a spiritual path.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Medea, falling in love with Jason against her duty to her father, argues with herself and confesses that she sees the better course and approves it, yet follows the worse.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid captures a lover driven by a force she recognizes as harmful to herself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also wonders at a grief that drives her where her dignity tells her not to go.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line; it fits being driven against one’s own judgement, but Medea is drawn toward a new love, not after one who has spurned her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pausanias says that a lover may beg and pray, swear oaths, sleep on the beloved’s doorstep and submit to a slavery no slave would accept, and yet gods and men excuse him because he is in love.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s speaker describes how lovers do humiliating things that would disgrace anyone not in love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wonders at the same humbling power: her grief makes her want to follow one who has turned away.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.R.M. Lamb)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a real passage; good fit on love excusing self-humiliation, though Pausanias treats it as a social convention rather than grief.

kurals.tamil:
நாணென ஒன்றோ அறியலம் காமத்தால்
பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanena ondroa ariyalam kaamaththaal
paeniyaar petpa seyin.
kurals.meaning: When the one I love, out of love, does what I long for, I no longer know anything called shyness.
kurals.elementary: When someone you love is kind to you and does just what you hoped, you forget to be shy around them. You just feel happy and close. The heroine says that is how she feels when her husband shows his love.
kurals.university: Here nāṇ (shyness, modesty) is not broken by force but forgotten: when pēṇiyār (the one I cherish) does peṭpa (what I desire) out of kāmam, ‘we do not know anything called shame’ (nāṇ eṉa oṉṟō aṟiyalam). The plural aṟiyalam can be inclusive (‘we women’) or the heroine’s own, and commentators differ on tense: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it conditionally (‘if he does…, we shall not know’), Solomon Pappaiah as past experience (‘when he did… I did not know shame’). Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘No sense of shame my gladdened mind shall prove, / When he returns my longing heart to bless with love’) takes it as a hope for his return. Read within the chapter, the couplet explains why reserve fails: in the presence of a loving husband, nāṇ has no place. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the last canto of the Gita Govinda, after Radha and Krishna are reunited, Radha playfully asks Krishna to paint her forehead mark, set her ornaments and arrange her hair, and he gladly does as she asks.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva ends his poem with a beloved who, with a loving partner, sets shyness aside entirely.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: when her beloved does what she desires, she knows no shyness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the closing canto, not checked against a translation this session; good fit on shyness forgotten in returned love, though the poem is also read devotionally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
christianity.explanation: In the garden before the fall, the first husband and wife stand before each other with no shame at all.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes the same freedom: in love returned, shame has no place.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close on the absence of shame between spouses, though Genesis describes innocence, not love-longing.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes husband and wife as each other’s garment: closeness, comfort and covering.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s couple share the same closeness: in mutual love, the wife no longer needs the cover of shyness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); shares the idea of spousal intimacy without barrier, but the verse is a ruling about the nights of Ramadan, not about shyness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song wishes she could show her love openly, without anyone thinking it shameful.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says that when her love is returned, she does not even feel shyness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); strong on wanting love free of shame, though the Song’s speaker is still constrained by convention.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nakula’s father and Nakula’s mother tell the Buddha that since they were married young they have never been unfaithful to each other even in thought, and that they wish to see each other in this life and in lives to come.
buddhism.explanation: The Anguttara Nikaya praises a lay couple whose love is open, mutual and wholehearted.
buddhism.tie_back: Their unguarded devotion parallels the Kural’s picture of love so mutual that shyness falls away.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a real sutta; it shares the ideal of mutual married love, but says nothing about shyness or its loss.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Come, let us enjoy pleasures, for it is a rare chance to be born a human being; after we have enjoyed pleasures, we shall enter on the path of the Ginas.”
jainism.explanation: Overcome by passion, the monk Rathanemi forgets his vows and the shame they should bring, and urges Rajimati to enjoy pleasures with him.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rathanemi forgets shame in desire; but the Jain text treats this forgetting as a fall, whereas the Kural sees it within a loving marriage.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match only, since the Jain frame condemns what the Kural accepts within marriage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho says the most beautiful thing is whatever one loves, and gives Helen as proof: she left behind her husband, her child and her parents and sailed to Troy, led astray by love.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho uses Helen to show that love can make a person forget every claim of propriety and family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also forgets shyness in love, though within her own marriage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment; it shares love’s power to sweep aside propriety, but Helen leaves her husband, which is the opposite of the Kural’s setting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal argues that the heart follows a logic of its own that calm reason cannot fully grasp.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds this in her own heart: when love is returned, the reasoned reserve of shyness simply disappears.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; paraphrase; cf. tr. W.F. Trotter)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line; next-best match, as Pascal speaks mainly of faith and says nothing about shyness.

kurals.tamil:
பன்மாயக் கள்வன் பணிமொழி அன்றோநம்
பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Panmaayak kalvan panimozhi androa-nam
penmai udaikkum padai.
kurals.meaning: Isn’t it the gentle, coaxing words of that thief of many tricks, my beloved, that serve as the army breaking down my womanly firmness?
kurals.elementary: Imagine building a strong sandcastle wall, and then a friend says something so sweet and kind that you happily knock the wall down yourself. The heroine says her husband’s gentle words are like that: they break down her strong ‘I won’t give in’ feeling.
kurals.university: The heroine calls her beloved pal-māyak kaḷvaṉ, ‘a thief of many wiles’, an affectionate reproach familiar from Tamil love poetry, and names his paṇimoḻi (humble, coaxing words) as the paṭai (army, weapon) that breaks her peṇmai (womanliness, here the firmness that resists). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peṇmai as a fortress (அரண்) and Solomon Pappaiah as the fort of self-restraint (மன அடக்கமாகிய கோட்டை), sustaining the military image of breaking. Puliyur Kesikan reads the couplet as past (‘were they not, on that day…’), referring to their courtship, while others read it as a present truth. Pope’s rendering on ytamizh.com (‘The words of that deceiver, versed in every wily art, / Are instruments that break through every guard of woman’s heart!’) pushes kaḷvaṉ toward ‘deceiver’, though the Tamil glosses keep the tone fond and playful. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth canto of the Gita Govinda, Krishna comes to Radha while she is still angry and pleads with her in the sweetest words, begging her to give up her anger and set her foot upon his head.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva shows a lover’s gentle, humble pleading overcoming a woman’s proud resistance.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna’s words are the Kural’s paṇimoḻi: coaxing speech that breaks down a woman’s firmness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canto, not checked against a translation this session; a close match on humble words melting resistance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb describes how smooth, flattering words can overcome a person’s resolve.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same idea: sweet, coaxing speech is the weapon that breaks down firmness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close on persuasive speech overcoming resolve, though the proverb warns against a seductress while the Kural speaks fondly of a husband.

islam.quote_or_event: “Some eloquent speech has the influence of magic.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet observed that well-chosen words can move people to do what they had refused to do.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same of her husband’s coaxing words, which work on her firmness like a spell.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong on the power of words to overturn resolve, though the hadith concerns public speeches rather than love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My beloved spoke, and said unto me: ‘Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.’”
judaism.explanation: The Song’s beloved wins the woman over with tender, coaxing words.
judaism.tie_back: In the Kural too, the beloved’s gentle words are what overcome the woman’s reserve.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); good fit on the beloved’s words drawing her, but there is no resistance being broken.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After the Buddha’s awakening, Mara’s three daughters, Craving, Discontent and Passion, approach him with flattering words and alluring forms to break his resolve, but he is unmoved.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta shows coaxing words used as a weapon against a person’s firmness, and the firmness holding.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same weapon of coaxing speech, but, unlike the Buddha, she gives way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a real sutta; the motif of words as a weapon against resolve fits, but the outcome is the reverse of the Kural’s.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Meekly and politely they approach him with their manifold arts to win his heart; and talking sweetly in confidential conversation they make him do (what they like).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that gentle, sweet speech is the means by which their resolve is overcome.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural names the same weapon, humble and sweet words used with many arts, as what breaks the heroine’s firmness.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close match on sweet words wearing down resolve, though the Jain text is a monastic warning and genders the danger the other way.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Hera borrows Aphrodite’s embroidered band, Homer says it holds love, desire, and the persuasive whispering that steals the wits even of the wise.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, lovers’ persuasive speech is literally a divine weapon that can overcome even Zeus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine names her beloved’s sweet words as the weapon that breaks her firmness, the same power Aphrodite’s band contains.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 14.214-217 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a strong match on seductive speech as a weapon against firmness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Gorgias argues that Helen cannot be blamed if she was persuaded by speech, because speech is a mighty lord that, with the smallest and least visible body, achieves the most divine works.
philosophy.explanation: Gorgias makes the power of persuasive words a defence of the one who yielded to them.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine offers a similar plea: it was her beloved’s coaxing words, a whole army, that broke her firmness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; close match on persuasive speech overpowering resistance.

kurals.tamil:
புலப்பல் எனச்சென்றேன் புல்லினேன் நெஞ்சம்
கலத்தல் உறுவது கண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pulappal enachchendraen pullinaen nenjam
kalaththal uruvadhu kandu.
kurals.meaning: I went meaning to sulk and hold back, but when I saw my heart already rushing to join him, I embraced him.
kurals.elementary: Imagine planning to stay grumpy with a friend who came back late. But when you see them, your heart feels so happy that you forget to be grumpy and give them a big hug instead. That is what happened to the heroine.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the Tamil love convention of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking or feigned pique): pulappal, ‘I will sulk’, was her plan, but pulliṉēṉ, ‘I embraced’, was the result, because she saw her neñcam (heart) already beginning kalattal (union, mingling) with him. The heart acting independently of the self continues the preceding chapter, neñcoṭu kiḷattal (‘speaking to one’s heart’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘my heart leaving me and joining him’, and Solomon Pappaiah elaborates that she stepped away to sulk but, seeing her heart go to him without restraint, gave up and embraced him. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss gives an allegorical (yogic) reading, a minority view. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; Pope’s rendering there (‘I’ll shun his greeting’; saying thus with pride away I went: / I held him in my arms, for straight I felt my heart relent) follows the standard reading.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha, who had held out against Krishna in wounded pride, is urged by her friend to go to him; she finally enters his bower, and her anger dissolves in the joy of seeing him.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem turns on Radha’s māna (proud sulking) giving way when she sees her beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation: she meant to sulk, but on seeing him her resolve melted into embrace.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s climax, not checked against a translation this session; a close fit on sulking dissolving at the sight of the beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go.”
christianity.explanation: After searching anxiously, the bride finds her beloved and holds him fast.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also ends up embracing the one she meant to hold off, because her heart has already gone to him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close on the embrace, though the bride has been searching, not sulking.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sees affection and mercy between spouses as a sign of God, a force that brings them back to calm together.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences that affection overriding her plan to sulk.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); shares the theme of spousal affection, but says nothing of a quarrel giving way.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.”
judaism.explanation: Esau, who had long held a grievance against Jacob, runs to him and embraces him the moment they meet.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a resolve to hold back gives way at the meeting, and an embrace takes its place.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a vivid match on resentment dissolving into embrace, though it is a reconciliation of brothers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that resentment ends only when it is met with its opposite.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds her small resentment dissolved not by argument but by her own heart’s affection.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a next-best match, since the verse concerns hatred generally while the Kural describes playful sulking that love overcomes.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Rathanemi had set out to win Rajimati, but on hearing her words his intention reverses and he returns to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rathanemi meets the other person intending one thing and does the opposite, though his reversal runs from passion to restraint, not from sulking to embrace.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match only, since the reversal runs in the opposite direction to the Kural’s.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus describes the secret of their bed, Penelope, who had held back from him in doubt, feels her knees and heart give way, bursts into tears, runs to him and throws her arms around his neck.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a wife’s long-guarded reserve dissolving in a single moment into an embrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s scene: she came holding back, but when her heart went to him she embraced him.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 23.205-208 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a close match on a wife’s reserve dissolving into embrace, though Penelope’s holding back is caution, not sulking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristophanes describes how the separated halves of the original human beings, longing for each other, run together and throw their arms about each other, wanting to grow into one.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s speaker presents love as an irresistible drive toward union with one’s other half.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s heart going to ‘mingle’ (kalattal) with her husband is this same drive toward union, which overrides her plan to sulk.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 191a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous myth; good fit on the urge to union, though Plato’s story has no element of sulking.

kurals.tamil:
நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்க்கு உண்டோ
புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ninandheeyil ittanna nenjinaarkku undoa
punarndhoodi niRpaem enal.
kurals.meaning: Can those whose hearts melt like fat thrown into the fire ever say, ‘We will be with him and still hold firm in our sulking’?
kurals.elementary: Put a pat of butter in a hot pan and it melts almost at once. The heroine says her heart is like that butter: the moment her husband is near, she cannot stay cross with him.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a vivid simile: niṇam tīyil iṭṭaṉṉa neñciṉār, ‘those whose hearts are like fat (niṇam) put into fire’, cannot say puṇarntu ūṭi niṟpēm, ‘we will unite and yet stand firm in ūṭal (sulking)’. Commentators differ over the construction: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘can those like me, with melting hearts, keep up a sulk once they have agreed to it’, Kalaignar takes it as ‘can they hold firm in sulking after having been together’, and Solomon Pappaiah expands it into a general statement about women whose hearts melt at the sight of their lovers. The couplet answers 1259 in general form and closes the chapter’s argument: with a heart like this, no niṟai can last. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the musical setting by P.A. Muthukrishnan reproduced on thirukkural.net paraphrases the image as butter in the flame (தழலிடை வெண்ணெய்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A devotee whose speech is sometimes choked up, whose heart melts, who cries continually and sometimes laughs, who feels ashamed and cries out loudly and then dances — a devotee thus fixed in loving service to Me purifies the entire universe.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a love so strong that the devotee’s heart melts and outward composure disappears.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has the same melting heart (dravate cittam), which leaves no room for holding back.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 11.14.24 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Srimad-Bhagavatam)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the melting heart and lost composure match, though the love here is devotion to God.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes a heart that has melted like wax, all strength gone.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses almost the same image, fat melting in fire, for a heart that cannot hold firm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a near match on the melting-heart image, though the psalmist melts in distress, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “The skins shiver therefrom of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts relax at the remembrance of Allah.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes hearts that soften and yield at the remembrance of God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has a heart that softens and yields the moment her beloved is near.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a next-best match on hearts softening, but the context is reverence for God, not love for a spouse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph made haste; for his heart yearned toward his brother; and he sought where to weep; and he entered into his chamber, and wept there. And he washed his face, and came out; and he refrained himself…”
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s heart melts at the sight of Benjamin, and he has to hurry away to weep before he can compose himself again.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks whether a melting heart can hold firm; Joseph barely manages it, and only by leaving the room.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); good fit on a heart that melts at the sight of a loved one, though it is a brother’s love and he does regain control.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred; there is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls passion the fiercest of fires.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows that fire at work: her heart melts in it like fat, unable to keep any resolve.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; fits the fire image, though the Buddha warns against the fire while the Kural describes surrender to it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A pot filled with lac thrown into the fire melts quickly and is destroyed; so monks are lost through intercourse with women.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the image of lac melting in fire for a monk whose resolve dissolves in the presence of desire.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s simile, fat melting in fire, applied to the same dissolving of firmness.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a striking match on the melting-in-fire image, though the Jain text is a monastic warning while the Kural speaks within marriage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid says Narcissus, consumed by love, wastes away as yellow wax melts before a gentle flame or as morning frost melts in the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid uses a melting image for a lover dissolved by passion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heart like fat in the fire is the same picture of a lover who cannot hold firm.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous simile; a close match on the melting image, though Narcissus’s love is for his own reflection.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza holds that an emotion can be restrained or removed only by an opposite and stronger emotion, not by knowledge or resolution alone.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza argues that a resolution cannot hold against a strong feeling unless a stronger feeling opposes it.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s plan to sulk is too weak against her melting love, just as Spinoza would predict.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known proposition; it explains why the heroine’s resolve fails, though Spinoza is not speaking of love specifically.
